item.title: 19. Cost programs that protect the business
item.description:
Module 2: Operating inside a portfolio company.
Key takeaways: - A cost program should be judged by net, realized, durable savings: start with the headline run-rate, then subtract costs to achieve, leakage, timing, and lost revenue. - In a freight brokerage, sort every cost into revenue-producing, loss-preventing (compliance, vetting, insurance), or true overhead, and protect the first two unless the sponsor and board choose otherwise. - Check the credit agreement's cap and conditions on run-rate savings addbacks, remember addbacks don't create cash, and involve legal early on layoffs, releases, WARN-type notice, and vendor termination terms.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-19.txt

item.title: 18. Pricing as a value creation lever
item.description:
Module 2: Operating inside a portfolio company.
Key takeaways: - A small price change flows almost directly to EBITDA, but you must turn the announced increase into a realized number by subtracting leakage, commissions, and volume loss, and checking timing. - Break-even math shows that price increases tolerate meaningful volume loss while price cuts demand large volume gains. Payment terms, accessorials, and customer mix are all part of price. - As COO and General Counsel, you protect pricing through contract terms, antitrust discipline, clean margin data, and incentive design, and you present it differently to the sponsor (realization), the board (risk), and lenders (durability and receivables).
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-18.txt

item.title: 17. Cash conversion and working capital programs
item.description:
Module 2: Operating inside a portfolio company.
Key takeaways: - Working capital is the cash tied up between paying carriers and collecting from shippers; cash conversion measures how much EBITDA becomes real cash after capital spending and working capital growth, so define it consistently with your sponsor and lenders. - Growth consumes cash, and a day improvement in DSO or DPO is mostly a one-time release, so budget working capital for growth, new branches, and customer terms, and favor process-driven gains over period-end timing. - As COO and General Counsel, you shape cash through customer and carrier contract terms, borrowing base eligibility, financing program treatment under the credit agreement, incentives, and data quality, and each of the sponsor, board, and lenders reads the result differently.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-17.txt

item.title: 16. Working effectively with operating partners
item.description:
Module 2: Operating inside a portfolio company.
Key takeaways: - An operating partner usually has influence rather than formal authority, so find out who they work for, who pays them, and route any real decision through the board, sponsor consent rights, and lender restrictions. - Test every proposed initiative by starting with the headline benefit, subtracting implementation costs, lost business, and working capital effects, and checking the covenant treatment, then present the realistic number to the sponsor, board, and lenders. - As General Counsel, check fees against affiliate-transaction and restricted-payment terms, manage confidentiality, conflict, and privilege risks, and keep side conversations from replacing the formal approval and forecasting process.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-16.txt

item.title: 15. Management incentive plans: equity, options, vesting, and ratchets
item.description:
Module 2: Operating inside a portfolio company.
Key takeaways: - Incentive equity, whether options, restricted stock, or profits interests, is a share of value created above a threshold, so its worth depends on the waterfall, debt, and any preferred stock, and it swings sharply with exit value. - Vesting, performance hurdles, ratchets, leaver terms, and acceleration decide who actually earns what, so definitions like cause and adjusted EBITDA need to be precise and stable. - As COO and General Counsel, keep promises tied to board-approved documents, check repurchase and payout obligations against the credit agreement, and hold back pool capacity for key hires.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-15.txt

item.title: 14. Budgeting and forecasting to sponsor and lender standards
item.description:
Module 2: Operating inside a portfolio company.
Key takeaways: - A budget is the approved annual commitment and a forecast is your current best estimate; in a PE-backed company you also need a cash forecast, and all three must use definitions that reconcile to the credit agreement and the monthly package. - Sponsors read your budget against the investment thesis, boards read it for risk and decisions, and lenders read it for covenant headroom and liquidity, so build a base case, a stress-tested downside, and a list of levers. - In a freight brokerage, a one-point gross margin slip or a working capital build can erase covenant cushion, so budget cash and leverage, not just EBITDA, and flag people, branch, and legal risks early with a bridge each time the forecast changes.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-14.txt

item.title: 13. The monthly reporting package, KPIs, and flash reports
item.description:
Module 2: Operating inside a portfolio company.
Key takeaways: - The monthly package combines the statements, an adjusted EBITDA bridge, cash and covenant tracking, and a few well-defined KPIs, and each audience (sponsor, board, lender) reads it for something different. - A flash report is judged by how close it lands to the final number, so build a repeatable estimating method, label it preliminary, and track flash-to-final variance every month. - Keep KPI definitions written and stable, tie every number to a source system, and reconcile every version of EBITDA and cash across board, lender, and diligence materials.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-13.txt

item.title: 12. Board governance in PE-backed companies
item.description:
Module 2: Operating inside a portfolio company.
Key takeaways: - A PE-backed board is small and sponsor-influenced, and significant decisions often clear three separate gates: a board vote, sponsor consent rights (reserved matters), and lender restrictions in the credit agreement. - Know your authority matrix and the order of approvals, because a hallway "yes" from the sponsor is not formal authorization, and signing before lender consent can leave you bound but unable to close. - Write decision memos that serve the sponsor, board, and lenders at once, keep minutes and privileged advice handled deliberately, and bring bad news before the next board meeting, not at it.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-12.txt

item.title: 11. The investment thesis and the 100-day plan
item.description:
Module 2: Operating inside a portfolio company.
Key takeaways: - An investment thesis is the sponsor's specific claim for why the company is worth buying and how it will grow in value, usually built on EBITDA growth and cash generation, with a higher multiple treated as a bonus. - The 100-day plan tests the thesis assumptions against reality and turns each pillar into an owner, metric, milestone, cost, working capital estimate, and list of legal, compliance, and people constraints. - Learn the thesis early, challenge unrealistic assumptions with data in the first weeks, and show how your functions affect each pillar in terms the sponsor, board, and lenders each care about.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-11.txt

item.title: 10. Valuation multiples and comparable companies
item.description:
Module 1: How private equity works.
Key takeaways: - A valuation multiple divides enterprise value by a metric like EBITDA, using comps from public companies and precedent deals, and it should be read as a range built from judgment, with matching periods (trailing versus forward) and definitions of adjusted EBITDA. - Because the multiple and your EBITDA multiply together, and debt is fixed, small changes in either swing equity value far more than enterprise value, so quality of earnings and credible positioning within the range matter. - Executives influence where the company lands in the range by documenting customer concentration, compliance record, retention, data quality, and standalone branch economics, and by remembering that multiples shift with the freight cycle and credit markets.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-10.txt

item.title: 9. Enterprise value versus equity value
item.description:
Module 1: How private equity works.
Key takeaways: - Enterprise value is the worth of the operating business to all capital providers; equity value is what remains for owners after net debt, debt-like items, preferred equity, and other senior claims. - Because debt is fixed, a ten percent change in enterprise value can move equity value by twenty percent or more, so small EBITDA cuts, multiple shifts, or reclassified liabilities hit owners hard. - Executives should know what counts as debt, debt-like items, and free cash in their credit agreement and any sale agreement, document trapped cash and legal or earnout exposures early, and keep working capital improvements process-driven rather than timing-driven.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-09.txt

item.title: 8. Free cash flow and working capital
item.description:
Module 1: How private equity works.
Key takeaways: - Free cash flow is EBITDA minus cash taxes, capex, and the increase in working capital (and cash interest for the levered version), so always confirm which definition a sponsor or lender is using. - In a freight brokerage, growth traps cash because receivables from shippers grow faster than payables to carriers, so a twenty percent revenue increase can turn twenty million of EBITDA into only a million or so of free cash. - Attach a working capital and payment-terms estimate to every growth plan, branch case, and contract, and improve cash through process rather than period-end timing, since lenders' borrowing bases and covenants depend on it.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-08.txt

item.title: 7. Reading the three financial statements like a sponsor
item.description:
Module 1: How private equity works.
Key takeaways: - Sponsors read the statements in a particular order: cash flow first, then the balance sheet to explain the gap between profit and cash, then the income statement to test the earnings story. - In a growing freight brokerage, receivables can grow faster than carrier payables, so strong EBITDA can still produce little free cash, as in the example where eight million dollars of EBITDA became one million. - Be ready to explain every large balance sheet and cash movement, and keep the statements, board reports, and lender definitions reconciled, because covenant calculations follow the credit agreement rather than GAAP.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-07.txt

item.title: 6. EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA, and the add-backs that get challenged
item.description:
Module 1: How private equity works.
Key takeaways: - EBITDA is a convention, not a GAAP measure, so adjusted EBITDA is only as good as the add-backs behind it. Buyers, lenders, and the board each test them differently, and buyers do it through a quality of earnings review. - Add-backs survive when they are truly non-recurring, documented, measurable, and applied consistently. Recurring "one-time" items, blended startup branch costs, and unrealized run-rate savings are the ones most often cut. - A gap between management's number and the diligenced number is multiplied by the exit multiple, so a five million dollar cut at ten times costs fifty million in value. Track one-time items as they happen, keep one reconciled bridge across all versions of EBITDA, and show how EBITDA converts to cash.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-06.txt

item.title: 5. IRR versus MOIC, and why sponsors watch both
item.description:
Module 1: How private equity works.
Key takeaways: - MOIC measures how many dollars come back per dollar invested but ignores time, while IRR is the annualized return that rewards getting cash back sooner, so sponsors watch both to judge size and speed. - The same multiple produces a lower IRR the longer the hold, and early distributions like dividend recaps raise IRR without changing MOIC, which is why timing and lender consent matter. - Executives should show payback timing for each initiative, understand that lenders care about cash and leverage rather than sponsor returns, and read management equity plans closely for how MOIC and IRR hurdles are defined.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-05.txt

item.title: 4. The three return levers: EBITDA growth, multiple expansion, and deleveraging
item.description:
Module 1: How private equity works.
Key takeaways: - Sponsor returns come from three levers: EBITDA growth, multiple expansion, and debt paydown. EBITDA growth is the most controllable, deleveraging depends on cash conversion, and multiple expansion is the least controllable, so disciplined sponsors treat it as a bonus rather than a plan. - In the example, ten million dollars of added EBITDA at a ten times multiple created one hundred million dollars of value, thirty million of debt repayment added thirty million more, and a one-turn swing in the exit multiple moved the result by thirty million either way. - Executives should show that EBITDA is high quality and backed by cash, including working capital in a brokerage, and tie each initiative to a timing case, because buyers discount low-quality earnings and lenders are repaid with cash, not EBITDA.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-04.txt

item.title: 3. The fund lifecycle and why the clock drives every decision
item.description:
Module 1: How private equity works.
Key takeaways: - A PE fund runs about ten years: roughly five years of investing, then a harvest period focused on exits, with possible extensions. Fees step down as it ages, so carry and realized cash matter more. - Time changes returns: the same 2.5 times money multiple is about a 20 percent IRR over five years but only about 14 percent over seven, and LPs judge the GP by cash returned (DPI) when it raises the next fund. - Know where your sponsor's fund is in its life, present initiatives with a timing case that shows payback before the likely exit window, and start legal, compliance, and retention readiness well before a sale.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-03.txt

item.title: 2. Fund economics: management fees, hurdle rates, carry, and the waterfall
item.description:
Module 1: How private equity works.
Key takeaways: - The management fee, often about two percent, pays the GP firm to operate and is usually charged on committed capital early on; the real upside is carry, typically twenty percent of profit, paid only after LPs clear a hurdle, often eight percent compounded. - In a waterfall, cash flows in order: return of capital, preferred return, GP catch-up, then an eighty-twenty split; whole-fund and deal-by-deal versions change when the GP gets paid and how much risk it has an incentive to take. - For an operating executive, carry is earned at exit, so timing, EBITDA quality, and clean numbers matter. Sponsor fees paid by your company are watched and capped by lenders, and the sponsor reads your results against the whole fund.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-02.txt

item.title: 1. GPs, LPs, and the anatomy of a PE fund
item.description:
Module 1: How private equity works.
Key takeaways: - A PE fund is typically a limited partnership: LPs supply capital passively and are liable only up to their commitment, while the GP makes the decisions and carries legal responsibility. - Capital is committed up front but called only as needed, and the closed-end fund runs about ten years, so your sponsor's behavior is shaped by where the fund sits in its life. - Your sponsor answers to LPs and reports valuations to them, and lenders lend to your company, not the fund, so understanding the fund helps you read board, lender, and capital-allocation decisions.
Transcript: https://rfortmeyer.github.io/sponsors-playbook/transcripts/lesson-01.txt
